frameworks.name: Push vs Pivot Decision Framework
frameworks.definition: Continue pushing on a business opportunity until a fundamental original assumption is proven false; if no core assumption is invalidated, the apparent losses are the cost of learning, not a signal to quit.

claims.text: Decide to push or pivot a business based on whether a fundamental original assumption has been proven wrong. Continue pushing until an assumption you started with is no longer true; if no original assumption is proven false, then losses are the cost of learning, not a failure signal.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: An invalidated assumption indicates the opportunity itself is flawed; unchanged assumptions indicate only execution errors remain solvable.
bounded_by: Does not apply when capital runway is exhausted and no new capital can be obtained
Does not apply when the original assumption was never clearly articulated

claims.text: In wholesaling, many people make significant income; a failing wholesaling business indicates a lead-generation problem, not a broken business model.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business generating revenue but at negative net profit
claims.mechanism: Wholesaling is a proven model with multiple successful practitioners; poor results in a proven model point to execution (lead source) rather than model viability.
bounded_by: Does not apply to unproven or experimental business models with no established success cases

claims.text: If a service or coaching business loses money in its core practice while teaching others how to do it, the ethical burden becomes significant regardless of profitability in adjacent businesses.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Coaching or service business where the coach is actively teaching others the practice
The coach has poor results in the domain they teach
claims.mechanism: Teaching a practice you lose money in undermines credibility and creates misalignment between what you teach and what you prove is possible.

claims.text: Wholesaling can be learned and scaled with no capital; beginners who add outside money before developing core skills often fail because they lack the execution discipline that no-money constraint forces.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder is new to the market (less than 2 years)
claims.mechanism: Having no capital forces the development of high-efficiency lead-generation and sales skills; early infusions of capital bypass this skill-building phase and create a false sense of progress that collapses when execution skills are needed.
bounded_by: Does not apply to capital-intensive industries where skill cannot substitute for capital
Does not apply to founders who have already developed the core execution skill in another domain

claims.text: Founders should learn a new business domain with zero external capital input; using only personal resources creates discipline and self-respect that funded shortcuts eliminate.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder attempting to learn a new business model they lack expertise in
Capital is available from other sources (existing business, investors, family)
claims.mechanism: Success achieved without external help creates confidence that external capital cannot replicate; founders who rely on capital for early wins will always wonder if they could have achieved the same result alone.
bounded_by: Does not apply when the business requires capital-intensive infrastructure (e.g., manufacturing, real estate development)
Does not apply when the founder has already proved the business model in another domain

claims.text: Learning a new field (e.g., wholesaling) without external help fundamentally changes a founder's confidence and risk posture permanently, creating a durable advantage not available to those who received capital support.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder has lost accumulated capital or status and rebuilt from zero
The loss and rebuilding occurred in a related business domain
claims.mechanism: Having experienced total loss and recovery with no external support removes fear-based decision-making from the founder's psychology; this enables confident decision-making in future downturns.
bounded_by: Does not apply to founders who have not experienced material loss
Does not apply to founders operating in completely unrelated domains from their loss experience

claims.text: A founder who has lost everything and rebuilt it themselves can make risky decisions with low fear, because they have proven they can recover from worst-case outcomes.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder has experienced material financial loss (loss of capital, business failure, significant drawdown)
claims.mechanism: Experiential knowledge that recovery is possible removes the primary source of risk anxiety (fear of permanent loss); this fear reduction enables higher conviction and better decision velocity.
bounded_by: Does not apply to founders who have not experienced material loss
Does not guarantee better business outcomes—lower fear improves decision velocity but not decision accuracy

examples.text: A real estate coaching business founder (Tammy) started a wholesaling business alongside her successful real estate investing practice. After one year, the wholesaling business had generated $250k in revenue but was operationally net-negative with hundreds of thousands in debt from poor marketing decisions and bad ROAS. The coaching business, which she started recently in response to customer requests, performed well in four months. The question became whether to continue the losing wholesaling business or focus entirely on coaching and real estate investing, where she had proven success.

A founder used external capital to enter wholesaling without first developing the core skills. The founder had access to money but lacked the lead-generation and sales discipline that the no-capital constraint would have forced. The result was rapid capital depletion. In contrast, founders who built wholesaling businesses from zero capital first developed the execution skills, then applied external capital later when they had already proven the model.

practices.text: When starting a new business domain you have no expertise in, prioritize learning free or low-cost lead generation methods (outbound calls, cold email, direct mail) before spending capital; the constraints will teach you execution discipline.
In a wholesale-style business, keep the best deals you source for yourself and flip the rest; this ensures you have a parallel revenue stream and proof of the model even as you scale.

If losing money in a practice you teach, develop a parallel business (real estate investing in Tammy's case) where you have track record and profitability; use that success to fund the coaching instead of the losing operation.
